transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me a little bit about what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Thank you so much for seeing me. It's really nice to meet you, too. 

Um, well, I guess I'm here because... it's actually a little embarrassing to admit, to be honest. I work as a camera operator and video editor, which I really love, and I'm usually pretty good at my job! But lately, I... well, what finally scared me into making an appointment is that I just keep making these really silly technical mistakes. Things I absolutely know better than to make. 

Like, just little slip-ups, like labeling camera cards wrong, or maybe missing a timecode note here and there. It's probably not the worst thing in the world, but recently I exported a client cut with the wrong lower-third on the screen, and I swear I had already checked it before sending it out. It just made me feel terrible, and I really want to make sure I'm doing a good job for my clients. 

I hope I'm explaining this okay... is that the kind of thing you were asking about?
Do you find that you struggle to maintain focus or make these kinds of careless mistakes in other areas of your life outside of work, such as with household chores or managing your personal finances?

Um, actually... no, I don't think so. I really try my best to keep on top of everything at home. I don't want you to think my whole life is a mess or anything! 

With my finances, I'm actually pretty careful. I always make sure things are paid on time because I'd just die of embarrassment if I messed up something important like my rent or credit cards. And with chores... well, I keep the house pretty tidy. I really like making sure my space is nice. 

So, no, I haven't really noticed those kinds of careless mistakes happening outside of my job, to be honest. Is... is that okay? I hope I'm answering this right. I just really haven't seen it happen with my personal stuff, and I want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.
Do you find that you spend a significant amount of your time feeling excessively worried or apprehensive about a wide range of different things, even when there isn't a specific reason to be?

Oh, um... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I definitely care about doing a good job, which is why that editing mistake bothered me so much, but... I don't really sit around worrying about everything for no reason. 

I actually try to stay pretty positive and upbeat most of the time! I really don't want to come across as a giant ball of stress or anything. I just... I mostly just get frustrated with myself when I mess up things I know I shouldn't. But as for just general worrying about a bunch of different things out of nowhere? No, not really. 

I hope that's a good thing? Does that make sense, or did I misunderstand the question?

When you make these mistakes, do you feel a strong, irresistible urge to go back and repeatedly check your work or perform specific rituals to make sure everything is 'just right' before you can move on?

Oh, no, I wouldn't say I do anything like that. I mean, I definitely try to double-check my work—especially lately, since I've been so worried about making those silly mistakes. I just want to make sure I'm giving my clients my best, you know? 

But I don't feel like... like I'm forced to do it, or like I have to do it a certain number of times or in a special way. I just take a quick look to make sure I didn't mess up the timecodes or the graphics again. Once I see it's okay, I'm good to go! 

I really don't have any, um, rituals or anything like that. I hope that's what you were asking? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture of what's going on.
Aside from the frustration you feel about these work mistakes, have you noticed a change in your overall mood, such as feeling down, hopeless, or less interested in the activities you usually enjoy?

Oh, no, definitely not! I'm really not a depressed person at all. I still love doing the things I usually do. Like, I still love going out with my friends and, um, watching movies and all of that. 

I don't want you to think I'm, like, sitting in the dark feeling sorry for myself! It's really just the work stuff that gets me down sometimes, just because I want to do a good job. But overall, my mood is totally fine. I'm usually a pretty happy person! 

Is it normal to just be frustrated about work but fine everywhere else? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right idea about how I'm feeling.
Did these mistakes at work start around the same time as any specific change, stressful event, or difficult situation in your life?

Well, um, I guess... yeah, it actually did. It's been going on at this level—where it's actually getting disruptive—for about two years and two months now. 

We had this big company readjustment back then, and it completely changed how my shoots and my edit reviews are run. I mean, it's a great company, and I'm really lucky to work there! I don't want to sound like I'm just complaining about my job or that I can't handle change. I promise I'm usually very flexible and a team player! 

It's just that the new workflow... I don't know, it just seemed to really throw me off my rhythm, and that's when these silly mistakes really started becoming an issue. Is it normal for a schedule change at work to affect someone like that? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right timeline and being helpful.

Looking back at that time when the company changed its workflow, would you say that the distress you felt or the impact these mistakes had on your life was significantly more intense than what most people would typically experience in that same situation?

Oh, um, no, I don't think so. I mean, I think my reaction was pretty normal? Everyone was a little stressed out when the new workflow started, honestly. It was a big adjustment for the whole team. 

I definitely don't think I was, like, falling apart or anything! I just got a little flustered, which I think anyone would when their routine gets turned upside down, right? I just tried my best to adapt and keep a positive attitude, like everyone else. I wouldn't say it was significantly more intense than what my coworkers were feeling. 

I hope that makes sense? I just want to make sure I'm not making it sound worse than it actually was. I'm really trying to give you an accurate picture.
Aside from your work frustration, have you been experiencing any physical symptoms lately, such as persistent feelings of exhaustion, muscle aches, or difficulty getting a good night's sleep?

Oh, no, definitely not! I'm really fortunate that way. I've always been pretty healthy and energetic. I don't really get muscle aches or anything like that, and I sleep just fine, mostly. 

I mean, sometimes I have a little trouble winding down at night because I'm just thinking about all the things I need to do the next day, but that's just normal stress, right? I'm definitely not walking around exhausted all the time. I wouldn't want you to think I'm not taking care of myself! 

I try to stay active and eat well, so physically, I feel great. Does that sound like what you'd expect? I just want to make sure I'm answering your questions the right way.
Even though you don't feel like you are worrying about a lot of different things, do you find that you often feel tense, restless, or on edge because of the pressure you feel at work?

Well, um, I guess I do get a little... restless sometimes? But I really don't think it's because I'm, like, overly anxious or anything bad! It's more just a physical thing, I think. 

Like, for example, when we have these long client screenings... I know I'm supposed to just sit quietly and watch the edits, but it almost feels like there's this pressure building up under my skin? Like my body is just telling me I really need to get up and do something, even though I know I'm supposed to just sit still and watch. 

I always do my best to keep it together, though! I'd never want to seem unprofessional in front of the clients or make it look like I'm not paying attention to their feedback. I just have a lot of energy, I guess, and sitting in a dark editing bay can make anyone a little stir-crazy, right? Is it okay that I feel that way sometimes? I just want to make sure I'm answering your question the right way and giving you what you need.
Looking back at your childhood or your time in school, do you remember feeling that same need to move around or difficulty sitting still when you were expected to be quiet and focused?

Well, um, I suppose I was a little bit like that as a kid, too. But I really wasn't a bad kid! I was just very enthusiastic, you know? 

I do remember in elementary school, my teachers actually had to move my desk a few times. I guess I had a habit of popping out of my seat a lot, or... or I would just blurt out the answers before I was called on. Sometimes I'd end up talking to my classmates or distracting them before I even realized what I was doing. 

But I really didn't mean to be disruptive! I just got so excited about what we were learning, or I just had so much energy I didn't know what to do with it. I always felt terrible if I bothered anyone. I hope that doesn't make me sound like I was a troublemaker? I always tried my best to be good and listen to the teachers, I promise. Is that the kind of thing you were asking about?

doctor.question: Looking back at your childhood or your time in school, do you remember feeling that same need to move around or difficulty sitting still when you were expected to be quiet and focused?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in elementary school, teachers moved my desk because I was always out of my seat, blurting answers, or bothering classmates before I realized I was doing it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms in childhood or time in school prior to age 12, specifically inquiring about feeling the need to move around or having difficulty sitting still when expected to be quiet.

patient.answer:
Well, um, I suppose I was a little bit like that as a kid, too. But I really wasn't a bad kid! I was just very enthusiastic, you know? 

I do remember in elementary school, my teachers actually had to move my desk a few times. I guess I had a habit of popping out of my seat a lot, or... or I would just blurt out the answers before I was called on. Sometimes I'd end up talking to my classmates or distracting them before I even realized what I was doing. 

But I really didn't mean to be disruptive! I just got so excited about what we were learning, or I just had so much energy I didn't know what to do with it. I always felt terrible if I bothered anyone. I hope that doesn't make me sound like I was a troublemaker? I always tried my best to be good and listen to the teachers, I promise. Is that the kind of thing you were asking about?

inference.note: The patient's reports of childhood symptoms (blurting out answers, difficulty sitting still, moving seats) combined with current difficulties with sustained attention, restlessness, and impulsivity (the 'pressure' to move) are highly consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive or combined type. Given the duration and childhood onset, adjustment disorders are now ruled out.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the primary reason for the patient's visit.
opening_question.question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me a little bit about what brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a history of hyperactivity and impulsivity dating back to childhood (blurting out answers, difficulty sitting still in school) and current symptoms of motor restlessness and difficulty remaining seated during professional tasks. While the patient does not report pervasive inattention in all life domains, the persistent pattern of hyperactive-impulsive symptoms since childhood, combined with current functional struggles linked to these traits, supports a diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation.
